title: East Franks
capsule: East Francia took shape at the Treaty of Verdun in 843, when the Carolingian empire was tripartitioned and Louis the German received the Germanic-speaking eastern lands — Saxony, Bavaria, Franconia, Alamannia, and eventually much of Lotharingia after the Treaty of Mersen (870). The kingdom was governed by Carolingian successors through Louis the Child (d. 911), whose death without issue broke the dynasty's hold; the magnates elected the Frankish duke Conrad I as king, a departure marking the hardening of East Francia as a distinct realm from West Francia. Under Conrad (r. 911–918) the eastern kingdom struggled against Magyar raids and ducal centrifugalism. At Conrad's death the crown passed to the Saxon Henry the Fowler, whose son Otto I's imperial coronation in Rome in 962 transformed East Francia into the nucleus of the Holy Roman Empire.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The core stem-duchy territories are well-attested through Carolingian diplomas, but exact frontier zones — especially in the Slavic marches and Lotharingia — shifted considerably and are only approximately mappable.
